📊 Visa finds 46% in Asia Pacific may use stablecoins by 2031 

📣 Stablecoin interest has moved well ahead of actual use across Asia Pacific, with 46% of surveyed consumers saying they are likely to use the tokens within five years compared with 16% who used them during the past year. The research found strong interest in using stablecoins for online purchases, travel, overseas shopping and moving money across borders. Yet the survey showed a large knowledge gap, with only 6% of respondents demonstrating what Visa described as an accurate understanding of how stablecoins work.

⭐️ Across the 14 markets, 46% of respondents said they were likely to use stablecoins during the next five years. Only 16% reported using them during the previous 12 months. Visa did not disclose in its release what those existing users had used stablecoins for. The 16% figure could therefore include trading, transfers, payments or other cryptocurrency activity and should not be treated solely as consumer payment adoption.

‼️ Cross-border transfers produced one of the strongest future-use readings. Around 49% of respondents said they thought stablecoins could become a common method of moving money between countries within five years. Visa Head of Digital Currencies for Asia Pacific Nischint Sanghavi said consumers were starting to consider stablecoins for “online purchases, travel and cross-border transfers.” The company views those uses as potential extensions of existing payment behavior.

Saylor believes the next major growth driver will be traditional banks. They’ll start issuing loans backed by BTC, just like they currently lend against real estate or stocks. In his view, this could be the biggest factor driving the price over the next three years.

Essentially, this process is already underway. The crypto lending market has grown to $67 billion, and major U.S. banks have already started offering Bitcoin-backed loans.

The market itself is also starting to pick up. BTC is up 40% this quarter alone, while Bitcoin ETFs saw another $2.4 billion in inflows last week.

OpenAI will label ChatGPT texts in the EU with an invisible watermark

On October 5, OpenAI announced that in the coming weeks it will add an invisible watermark to the texts of ChatGPT and Codex for users in the European Union. The company links this move to the EU law requirement for artificial intelligence to label generated text in a way that can be recognized by machines. On the same day, clients using the software interface worldwide can enable labeling for individual models. By default, it is turned off in the interface. The company does not make it a global standard for ChatGPT at the outset.

The technology is called textGrain. It alters the statistics of word choices where models have multiple options and does not add hidden characters, invisible spaces, or unusual punctuation. The detector looks for this signal in a prepared excerpt. The watermark is not tied to a person, organization, account, request, or correspondence and does not indicate which part of the text was written by a person.

OpenAI explicitly limits the reliability of verification. At a target false positive rate of 1%, the detector found the watermark in about 80% of excerpts of 200 tokens and about 95% of excerpts of 400 tokens in texts like psychological ones. In mathematics, where word choice is stricter, the result was notably lower. Editing weakens the signal: in the assessment of 400-token excerpts, replacing 10% of words with synonyms reduced detection from about 92% to 66%, and replacing 25% of words decreased it to 17%. The absence of the watermark, according to the company's statement, does not prove that the text was written by a person. It could be short, edited, translated, created before the labeling was launched, or by another system.

Anthropic has been labeling texts of the new Claude models since August. According to the company's documentation, for models released in the EU on August 2, 2026, and later, a machine-readable label is applied from day one, and this labeling is effective not only in the EU but also wherever Claude is available. There is a transitional period for old models.

The assertion that the content can be identified within seconds has been removed: OpenAI's message does not mention a verification time. The wording that the system can only be bypassed by manually replacing words with synonyms has been removed. The company writes that such replacement weakens detection but does not state it as the only method and does not promise that the watermark disappears completely after it. The word "humanizing" in the source material does not relate to the described technology. Verification: OpenAI's message from October 5, 2026, section about textGrain limitations.
